exercise.name: Crunch (Hands Overhead)

reference.title: Crunch (hands overhead)
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Body weight, exercise type Strength

exercise.mechanics: Isolation (spinal flexion, mostly thoracic; long lever)

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl up, inhale as you lower. Do not hold the breath at the top.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up, a short squeeze, about 1.5 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1 s up, brief pause, 1.5-2 s down
prescription.progression: Slower lowering and a 2 s hold, then a light dumbbell held overhead

cues.text: Lie on your back, knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat. Reach the arms straight overhead, biceps beside the ears, hands close together.
Breathe out and curl the head, shoulders and shoulder blades off the mat; the arms travel with the trunk, not ahead of it.
Short squeeze at the top. Low back stays on the mat, ribs pulled down.
Breathe in and lower slowly, shoulder blades first, head last; arms stay beside the ears.
Rest the head briefly and repeat without swinging the arms.

mistakes.mistake: Swinging the arms forward to throw the trunk up
mistakes.fix: Keep the arms locked in line with the upper trunk; let the abs do the lift.

mistakes.mistake: Ribs flaring and the low back arching at the start
mistakes.fix: Exhale and draw the ribs down before you curl; bend the elbows if the shoulders are tight.
Look up toward the ceiling just ahead of the knees.
Stop once the shoulder blades clear the mat.

kinematics.measure: Upper trunk (T12 to C7) from the floor
kinematics.norm: Head, shoulders and shoulder blades clear the mat; no study fixes the angle (clinical opinion)
Small: about 3 degrees of lumbar flexion in a crunch, cited by Escamilla 2016 from earlier work
Most of the curl happens here (clinical opinion)
Straight overhead in line with the trunk: the longest arm lever, which raised abdominal activity (Crommert 2021)
Knees about 90 degrees, feet flat; the pelvis and legs do not move (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 1 s up and 1.5-2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: Crommert, Bjerkefors, Tarassova and Ekblom 2021, abdominal muscle activation during common modifications of the trunk curl-up exercise (J Strength Cond Res 35(2):428-435; PMID 29319600)
Escamilla, Lewis, Pecson, Imamura and Andrews 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379; PMC4922527)
Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.

Low-back pain, disc problems or flexion intolerance: start with a McGill-style curl-up, dead bug or plank; partial curl-ups gave the best abdominal challenge for the least spine compression in one model study (Axler and McGill 1997).
Shoulder pain or limited overhead mobility: bend the elbows or bring the hands to the temples.
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion work.
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion and twisting.
The athlete mesh rests on the mat; the rig collision shapes are thicker than the mesh at the back and buttocks, so floorTolerance records how far those proxy shapes sink below the mat surface.
modify: Neck strain: hands behind the head (standard crunch).
Tight shoulders: arms angled up toward the ceiling instead of flat overhead.
regressions: Crunch with the hands behind the head.
Crunch with the arms crossed on the chest.
progressions: Slow 3 s lowering with a 2 s hold.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the ribs toward the pelvis. Moving the arms to load the curl-up (the overhead position is the longest lever) raised activity in all the abdominal muscles studied (Crommert 2021); a plain crunch is about 53% upper and 39% lower rectus MVIC (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: External and internal obliques assist trunk flexion and rise with the arm load (Crommert 2021).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: External and internal obliques assist trunk flexion and rise with the arm load (Crommert 2021).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Stay quiet: rectus femoris is only about 6% MVIC in a crunch (Escamilla 2016). They only steady the bent legs.
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Stay quiet: rectus femoris is only about 6% MVIC in a crunch (Escamilla 2016). They only steady the bent legs.
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_r: Holds the straight arms up beside the ears as the trunk curls (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_l: Holds the straight arms up beside the ears as the trunk curls (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.lats_r: Lengthened overhead; they steady the arms and ribs (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.lats_l: Lengthened overhead; they steady the arms and ribs (clinical opinion).
